items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.original_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_description: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:06 Insurers aren't avoiding AI due to fear—they're waiting for core platform vendors to deliver native capabilities instead of risky integrations. October 22, 2026 Image We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI; they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase; it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. What This Means If You're Evaluating Tools Right Now A few things are worth doing before you sign anything: Separating "edge" AI from "core" AI. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. Testing whether the value is domain-specific. James Ballot Diane Brassard October 22, 2026 We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. items.rss_description: The Insurance Alignment Gap: Where Insurer Priorities and Customer Protection Needs Converge…and Diverge RyanMeyer Wed, 10/21/2026 - 10:47 Insurers are modernizing for efficiency, while customers seek affordability, trust, and protection. This report reveals how closing the alignment gap can create lasting value. October 21, 2026 Image Insurers are prioritizing cost reduction, profitability, modernization, and AI. Customers are looking for something different: affordability, trust, preparedness, and protection that feels relevant to the risks they face every day. This growing alignment gap matters. Modernization and AI investments deliver their full value only when customers see and feel the benefit. When insurer priorities and customer expectations drift apart, confidence erodes, and so does the opportunity to help customers build financial resilience. Based on original research with both insurers and insurance customers, this report examines where priorities align, where they diverge, and how insurers can connect business transformation to customer value. It explores three areas that matter most to building confidence and resilience: Relevance. Customers want protection that reflects their everyday risks. Learn how insurers can deliver coverage that feels meaningful and worth the cost. Personalization. Tailored products, pricing, and communications help customers feel understood and prepared. Learn how personalization supports trust. Digital engagement. Digital experiences shape how customers perceive their insurer. Learn how to use them to strengthen confidence and connection. Whether you lead strategy, product, distribution, customer experience, or technology, this report offers a research-based view of what customers expect and how your transformation priorities can meet them. Read the Report Sponsored by Majesco ITL Partner: Majesco

items.extracted_text: USAA secures 56% upsized $350m Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond priced below guidance - Artemis.bm USAA secures 56% upsized $350m Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond priced below guidance - Artemis.bm USAA secures 56% upsized $350m Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond priced below guidance 23rd October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard USAA has now priced and secured the 56% upsized target of $350 million of multi-year per-occurrence reinsurance coverage from its new Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited (Series 2026-2) catastrophe bond issuance, getting the capital markets coverage at pricing levels below guidance, Artemis can report. USAA returned to the catastrophe bond market earlier this month to sponsor its 48th cat bond that we have tracked from the company. Initially, the target was to secure $225 million of multi-year per-occurrence reinsurance coverage, but in our first update, we learned that USAA had lifted the target size by 56% to $350 million, while the price guidance was also lowered for the three tranches of notes on offer. We then reported in our update yesterday that the $350 million target remained, but USAA was still looking to capitalise on investor appetite, with the price guidance lowering once again for each of the tranches on offer. Now, we can report that USAA successfully finalised its latest cat bond sponsorship to provide the 56% upsized $350 million of multi-year per-occurrence reinsurance protection, while the pricing was finalised at a below initial guidance level for all three tranches of notes. We won’t repeat all the details of the cat bond in our updates on size and pricing, so make sure to visit the Artemis Deal Directory entry for more background details on the transaction . Once settled, all three tranches of Residential Reinsurance 2026-2 cat bond notes will provide USAA with four years of multi-peril per-occurrence catastrophe reinsurance protection on an indemnity trigger basis, running from December 1st, 2026, through to November 30th, 2030. The Class 2 tranche of notes will provide USAA with $100 million of reinsurance protection with an initial base expected loss of 6.04%. These notes were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance of 8.5% to 9.25%, which was lowered to 7.75% and 8.5%, and then fell again to 7.25% to 7.75%, eventually pricing at the lowest end of 7.25%. A further tranche of Series 2026-2 Class 3 notes will also provide USAA with $100 million of reinsurance protection. These notes have an initial base expected loss of 3.34% and were initially offered to investors with price guidance of 5% to 5.5%, which later reduced to 4.25% and 5%, and then fell to a tighter spread of 3.75% to 4.25%, eventually pricing at 4%. The final $150 million Class 5 tranche of Series 2026-2 notes that Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited will issue have an initial base expected loss of 1.43%. These notes were initially marketed with price guidance of 2.5% to 3%, which again, was lowered in our first update to 2% and 2.5%, and fell further to 1.75% to 2%. We’re now told by sources that the notes have been priced to pay investors an initial risk interest spread of 2%. This is a great result for USAA. The insurer has managed to secure its latest catastrophe bond with more reinsurance than initially sought, while pricing well below the initially expected guidance ranges. With a staggering 48 catastrophe bond transactions from USAA now detailed in our extensive Deal Directory, the insurer and its now 47 deal strong Residential Re cat bond program is the most prolific sponsor and program in the cat bond market. You can read all about this new Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited (Series 2026-2) catastrophe bond from USAA and every other cat bond transaction in the extensive Artemis Deal Directory . Munich Re said today that the third-quarter of 2026 saw strong financial […] Munich Re raises full-year 2026 profit target as Q3 result well-above consensus was published by: www.Artemis.bm Our catastrophe bond deal directory Sign up for our free weekly email newsletter here .
items.extracted_text: Munich Re raises full-year 2026 profit target as Q3 result well-above consensus - Artemis.bm Munich Re raises full-year 2026 profit target as Q3 result well-above consensus - Artemis.bm Munich Re raises full-year 2026 profit target as Q3 result well-above consensus 23rd October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Demonstrating the continued profitability of reinsurance underwriting businesses in 2026, global giant Munich Re has preliminarily reported its third-quarter net profit will be higher than consensus at €1.7 billion, on which basis the company has raised its full-year profit guidance by €300 million. Munich Re said today that the third-quarter of 2026 saw strong financial performance for the company, resulting in a net profit projected to be €1.7 billion, much higher than the analyst consensus estimate of €1.479 billion. The reinsurance company has delivered “pleasing operating performance across all business segments,” Munich Re explained. This has been helped by major losses being below expectations for its P&C reinsurance business, while investment results have also been strong. Munich Re, like the other large re/insurers can be expected to report in their Q3 results, further demonstrates the benefits of operating a large, globally diverse insurance and reinsurance underwriting operation. The profit target beat shows how the business model can remain a very profitable venture in an environment where major loss experience remains low, despite the recent steep price declines that are being seen in the softening market environment. In times when underwriting results remain strong but the market is softening, major reinsurers tend to take the opportunity to bolster their reserves. Munich Re seems to be highlighting this today, saying that subject to major loss activity it “intends to continue strengthening its balance sheet where appropriate in the fourth quarter.” The net result will now reach €5.7 billion for the first nine months of this year for Munich Re. As a result, with this above the previous target that was expected, Munich Re has now raised its full-year 2026 profit target by €300 million, from €6.3 billion to €6.6 billion. Munich Re’s performance shows how reinsurance profits continue to flow, helped considerably by the fact major loss activity has remained below averages year-to-date. This reads across positively for reinsurance strategies in the insurance-linked securities (ILS) market as well, where performance also remains attractive despite the softening of property catastrophe rates. Munich Re was already running at record levels of profit after the first-half of this year , although at that stage it maintained its earlier full-year target. But now with the US hurricane season running so far loss-free, this has likely been one factor that gives the reinsurer the confidence to lift its guidance. items.extracted_text: Insurance-linked securities attract DACH investor interest, allocations to rise: BAI survey - Artemis.bm Insurance-linked securities attract DACH investor interest, allocations to rise: BAI survey - Artemis.bm Insurance-linked securities attract DACH investor interest, allocations to rise: BAI survey 23rd October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans A survey of 105 institutional investors across the DACH-region undertaken by the German association for alternative investments, shows that an increasing number of allocators in the region are choosing catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities, while more indicate they intend to enter the sector. The German association for alternative investments, the BAI or the Bundesverband Alternative Investments e.V., is the cross-asset and cross-product interest group for alternative investments in Germany. The organisations annual survey highlights why institutional investors in the DACH-region (Germany, Austria, and Switzerland) invest in private markets and alternative strategies, as well as where there focus will be in the future. There are a number of interesting data points relevant to catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities as an alternative asset class, most important of which are the rising investor allocations to and interest in ILS assets. The BAI asked investors what alternative asset classes they are already invested in, with ILS one of the categories. In 2025 the response was 9% of surveyed institutional investors were allocating to ILS, but in the new 2026 survey this figure has risen to 11%. Promisingly, the BAI’s survey also adds on data for the planned entries of new investors to an asset class over the next twelve months (the Outlook in the chart below), which raises the figure to 14%, assuming those already allocated to ILS maintain those investments. The BAI said that the survey shows that in general, “Investors are deepening what they already own rather than expanding extensively into new asset classes.” Notably though, on the increase of 3% from 2026 to the Outlook, ILS does compare well with only infrastructure debt having a higher percentage increase in its Outlook (in the chart above). Interestingly, the BAI breaks out hedge funds and liquid alternatives as its own asset class, which of course some might place catastrophe bond funds in, given they can have attractive liquidity for allocators, depending on the fund structure. The BAI said, “Hedge Funds and Liquid Alternatives are back. After years at the margins, adoption climbed from 15 % to 21 % and is expected to reach 23 %, showing sustained momentum across all three periods.” On average, insurance-linked securities (ILS) stacks up well, as an asset class that is attracting increasing investor interest among institutional allocators in the DACH region. But allocations remains small so far, which is typical given most investors only commit a small percentage of their overall assets to cat bonds and ILS. The BAI survey found that the average allocation of already invested LPs, among those polled, into cat bonds and ILS is 2.6%. When looking across the entire surveyed institutional portfolio, which equates to €2.9 trillion in total AuM held by the LPs, just 0.1% is allocated on an AUM weighted basis. But, as a straight percentage of the total institutional portfolio, allocations to ILS and cat bonds have increased, from 0.2% in 2025 to stand at 0.3% in the 2026 survey results. Which shows the potential for more assets to flow from investors in the DACH region to the ILS asset class over-time, as awareness and interest keeps rising. items.extracted_text: AM Best Revises Outlook to Stable for Ohio Mutual Insurance Group’s Members Article 0 Comments AM Best has revised the outlook to stable from negative for the Long-Term Issuer Credit Ratings (Long-Term ICR) and affirmed the Financial Strength Rating (FSR) of A (Excellent) and the Long-Term ICRs of “a+” (Excellent) for the members of Ohio Mutual Insurance Group (OMIG) based in Bucyrus. The outlook of the FSR is stable. The ratings reflect OMIG’s balance sheet strength, which AM Best assesses as strongest, as well as its strong operating performance, neutral business profile and appropriate enterprise risk management. The revision of the Long-Term ICR outlook to stable from negative reflects the improvement in OMIG’s operating performance resulting from management initiatives implemented over the past few years. Following consecutive underwriting losses in 2022 and 2023, attributable to an unusually high level of catastrophe losses and increased loss severity due to rising inflation, OMIG’s management implemented initiatives to support future profitability. Management has addressed this volatility through rate increases and inflation adjustments, aggressive re-underwriting of the book of business, the non-renewal of certain policies, in-depth inspections and higher deductible requirements. These actions have led to improved performance in subsequent years. OMIG has remained profitable in 2026 despite the impact of a large catastrophe that absent these initiatives would have had a greater effect on the group. The continued improvement as these initiatives have taken hold demonstrates that the actions are sustainable and effective. AM Best expects these actions to continue to sustain OMIG’s strong operating performance and align results with historical performance. items.extracted_text: AM Best: Social Inflation Drives Surge in Commercial Auto Liability Claims Article 0 Comments According to recent report from AM Best, commercial auto liability insurance coverage has continued to bear the brunt of rising litigation costs, outpacing economic inflation. Social inflation has negatively affected commercial auto liability ultimate claim costs for several years, which is evident by looking at average claim severity. Economic inflation from 2014 to 2024 averaged 2.8% annually. Over the same period, commercial auto liability insurance loss payments for the first 12 months have trended upward at 6.4% annually—more than double the annual increase of economic inflation, AM Best said. AM Best defines social inflation as the rising cost of insurance claims that exceeds general economic inflation, driven by societal and legal trends like higher jury awards, increased litigation, and expanded definitions of liability. AM Best Special Report: Social Inflation Adds Pressure to US Property/Casualty Liability Results Commercial auto liability losses are capped by policy limits, typically $1 million. Individual auto claims resulting in loss payments exceeding that threshold will fall to an umbrella policy if that type of coverage is in place. Through 2018, umbrella pricing tracked closely with general liability pricing. However, as social inflation began to impact commercial auto claims, and those claims spilled into umbrella coverages, the pricing on the latter has diverged from general liability, becoming more costly, and has yet to return to its prior level. Historically, umbrella pricing followed closely with general liability but more recently, David Blades, associate director at AM Best said, “As social inflation began to impact commercial auto claims, and those claims spilled into the umbrella coverage, umbrella pricing diverged from general liability, becoming more costly.” Among the report’s other highlights: Claims being open longer leaves more exposure to jury precedent, in addition to most likely resulting in elevated claim adjustment expenses. After adjusting for settlement rates, commercial auto claim frequency has increased over the past 10 years, which also creates a gap in what has been paid and what is expected to be paid. Tort reforms may help. Sweeping tort reforms in Florida have helped offset excessive litigation costs, resulting in average paid claim severity to trend downward. Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: Phoenix Hit by Hail and Strong Winds, Damaging Vehicles Across Valley Article 0 Comments Arizona is not usually known as a hot spot for severe weather, but this week the state experienced hail, flooding and even a rare tornado. A severe storm on Wednesday produced hail the size of golf balls in metro Phoenix, damaging cars windshields across the Valley. Reports on social media showed vehicle windshields destroyed by hail. North Phoenix, Glendale, Tempe and Mesa were among the Valley communities that felt the worst of the hail. Winds of up to 60 mph were responsible for downed trees across the metro. While hailstorms are infrequent in Phoenix, the metro has experienced multiple severe storms in the past year, including a November 2025 storm that produced hail in the West Valley. In October 2010, Phoenix was hit by successive hailstorms that caused an estimated $2.7 billion in insured losses. The worst of the severe weather on Wednesday missed Phoenix to the north. Communities near Prescott and Flagstaff saw extensive damage caused by winds of up to 70 mph and heavy rainfall. Overgaard, which is part of Navajo Country, reported heavy damage from strong winds. Local reports suggested a possible tornado hit the community, but the National Weather Service has not yet confirmed whether a tornado is responsible. Dry conditions are expected across most of the state in the coming days. items.extracted_text: Chubb CEO Greenberg: Industry Has to ‘Put Arms Around’ AI Liability Article 0 Comments The insurance industry has dealt with emerging risks in the past, and Chubb CEO Evan G. Greenberg said he thinks the same approach can be applied to the rapid escalation of apparent liabilities presented by business’ use of artificial intelligence. Speaking during a conference call to discuss third quarter earnings, Greenberg was asked about insurance coverage for AI liability. Evan G. Greenberg “As an industry, we have to put our arms around this,” he said, adding that the industry “had to do this with emerging liabilities over the last 50 years, and there’s a pretty good template to follow.” Greenberg described AI liability as a “growing and emerging exposure” which is “not contemplated in casualty underwriting to date.” He said he can imagine “a combination of coverage clarifications, ultimately – exclusions and separate AI-related liability coverages.” “This will all emerge along with underwriting and pricing to discern between risks,” he added. “AI-related liability exposures will vary between insureds and type of insureds…to assist businesses generally and add to greater certainty overall in the liability environment as it emerges.” Greenberg went on to contemplate the materialization of some certification standards – best practices in the use and management of AI and agentics to also assist in insurance underwriting. At Chubb, Greenberg said the insurer has governance and management to protect the data it holds, as well as its agentics and large language models. Best practices consider “how we control and limit what they can do, where they can do it, how they can do it, how we instruct for it – and then protect our own perimeter [with] multiple layers of detection and defense against third-party or external use of agentics and AI that could imperil Chubb’s data or systems. “We invest significantly in this. We pay very close attention to it,” the CEO said. Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: Catastrophe bond market to hit second $20bn+ issuance year at fastest pace yet - Artemis.bm Catastrophe bond market to hit second $20bn+ issuance year at fastest pace yet - Artemis.bm Catastrophe bond market to hit second $20bn+ issuance year at fastest pace yet 23rd October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans As the catastrophe bond market pipeline builds for the fourth-quarter of 2026, we are already tracking what will be only the second ever year where issuance of 144A catastrophe bonds and private cat bond deals has exceeded the $20 billion level, while currently the market remains on a faster issuance pace than 2025. Catastrophe bond market participants had entered 2026 with a view that the $20 billion of issuance milestone would be seen again this year. Following on from the landmark record year of cat bond issuance in 2025, when we tracked over $25.6 billion of issuance, across full Rule 144A and private cat bond deals ( see our quarterly cat bond market reports for all the details ), the expectation has always been that the market would continue to see a $20 billion plus level of issuance. There are a number of reasons growth of the cat bond market persists and had always been expected to continue. For one, the growing number of sponsors in the market and especially new or first time cat bond sponsors, shows that the adoption of cat bond-backed reinsurance continues to grow, which is a significant input and influence for higher issuance volumes. We track first-time cat bond sponsors by quarter and year in this chart . In addition to the growing number of sponsors in the catastrophe bond market, the fact we’ve seen a prolonged period of market growth has meant that there are rising levels of maturities coming due, which delivers meaningful cash for cat bond fund managers to redeploy, another factor that continually fuels market expansion. We track upcoming catastrophe bond maturity volumes by quarter and month in these charts . The cat bond investor base currently has plenty of cash to put to work after a summer of strong coupon returns. As we reported recently, just the UCITS cat bond fund sector grew its combined assets by roughly $1 billion through the third-quarter of the year , a period when capital raising slows, but seasonal returns drive cash levels higher. With UCITS just a segment of the market, it means cat bond coupon earnings may have accumulated more than $2 billion of cash for investors to deploy during Q3 alone. Add to that the fact the investor base continues to expand, while multi-strats, hedge funds and other fixed income managers continue to include cat bonds as an investable asset class in their fund prospectuses, all means the market is well-primed. All of these factors position the market for another very strong year, with the full-year record still in sight, although still requiring one of the busiest final quarters of the year ever so records are not assured. As things stand today in 2026, we’ve tracked over $18.92 billion of settled cat bond issuance , across 144A cat bonds and private deals, while the building market pipeline is now targeting issuance of a further $1.3 billion of cat bond notes in the coming weeks. Which means, based on Artemis’ data, if all that planned pipeline issuance settles as currently targeted, issuance looks set to surpass the $20 billion mark and hit approximately $20.22 billion around the week of November 9th, across 144A cat bonds, the private cat bonds we’ve tracked and the pipeline we have visibility of today. In terms of how that compares to the pace of issuance in 2025, impressively even against the high-bar last year set 2026 is still running at a faster pace . Last year, the cat bond market surpassed the $20 billion level of issuance for the first time ever on November 25th 2025 with two deals settling, which took volumes over that milestone both for 144A cat bonds alone and for 144A plus private cat bonds. So, with the latest information we have projecting that $20 billion will be reached in the week of November 9th, the potentially record-setting pace continues. Currently, we project Rule 144A cat bond issuance on its own will reach $19.82 billion during the week of November 9th, so there is every chance that the 144A cat bond market also hits $20 billion of issuance earlier in 2026, than it did during the record year seen in 2025. Breaking the market down to Rule 144A property catastrophe bond issuance only, the $20 billion milestone was only reached on December 16th in 2025. This year, we project that 144A property cat bond issuance may be at or around $19.4 billion the week of November 9th, so this record may also fall in 2026. There is still a way to go before we can start looking at full-year record potential for 2026. As we explained in our latest quarterly cat bond market report , we need to see $6.7 billion of new cat bond issuance to set an annual record this year. In fact, for 2026 to see record total catastrophe bond issuance, we will need the fourth-quarter to see the second highest level of issuance ever, after last year’s $7 billion. But, sources suggest that is possible, although by no means guaranteed at this stage. It’s worth noting though, that pipeline deals are already upsizing and pricing down, with conditions in the cat bond market extremely conducive at this time for sponsors seeking attractive deal execution and well-priced reinsurance from the capital markets. So all the necessary factors are there and ready to support a record year. Now it simply comes down to deal-flow and whether enough sponsors recognise the current positive catastrophe bond market opportunity. items.extracted_text: Fronting companies to engage more frequently with ILS market: AM Best - Artemis.bm Fronting companies to engage more frequently with ILS market: AM Best - Artemis.bm Fronting companies to engage more frequently with ILS market: AM Best 23rd October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Rating agency AM Best has indicated in a new report that fronting companies are expected to engage more frequently with the insurance-linked securities (ILS) market to drive capacity diversification using catastrophe bonds, sidecars and collateralized reinsurance structures. In its report, AM Best notes that the property and casualty fronting market continued to grow at a healthy rate during 2025, driven in part by the sustained expansion of MGA-oriented business. The agency highlighted how fronting has expanded over time to include much broader sets of entities, such as managing general agents (MGAs). The agency further clarified that over the last couple of years, there has been a trend for some fronts to assume business from a variety of entities, including other insurers, reinsurers, and state facilities. Data from the report shows that as of year-end 2025, market estimates suggest upwards of $30 billion of US P&C insurance industry premium is fronted, which heavily showcases how the fronting market has continued to grow at a rapid pace. “As of year-end 2025, the fronting specialists assumed premium totaled $4.8 billion, up significantly from the $1.8 billion recorded in 2024. Of the $4.8 billion in assumed premiums written in 2025, about $1.7 billion was unaffiliated assumed premium, representing written premium that would present a different risk profile for these fronting companies since it is business initially underwritten by other companies,” AM Best explained. The agency further noted that capacity diversification is likely to persist, as fronting companies are expected to engage with the insurance-linked securities market on a more frequent basis. “For ILS investors, fronting companies act as efficient transformers so they can access risks through rated insurance companies directly, getting them closer to the risk,” AM Best said. “These transactions offer a different risk profile compared to the traditional catastrophe risks that make their way to the ILS market. The differences in risk profile also creates uncertainties. While catastrophe risks are typically short-tailed, these risks are longer-tailed, incorporate investment assumptions, and adverse reserve developments and loss estimates could lead to operational conflicts between the fronting company and the investors. “Fronting companies would also need to have specific fall-back plans on what to do after the commutation date.” In recent years, fronting has become a common practice in the ILS market. Investors and ILS funds team up with fronting insurers to access risk more efficiently, simultaneously leveraging the fronting provider’s established credit rating, while utilising the provider’s ability to hold onto the tail risk associated with the transaction. The report further explained that MGAs are drawn towards fronting companies due to reinsurance efficiency and optionality, while simultaneously highlighting multi-year capacity stability, accelerated product development and distribution capabilities, and enhanced access to reinsurance and the capital markets as key advantages. As the capital markets provide substantial alternative pools of liquidity, this allows MGAs to underwrite larger volumes of business and access capacity for bigger risks than traditional insurance capacity would normally allow. The rating agency also observes that the majority of fronting companies are capital light vehicles backed by private equity. “Almost half of the fronting organizations are owned by private equity, which has been attracted by the fee-based revenue, capital-light vehicles, and limited balance sheet risk. The breadth of the other owners, which include insurance companies, brokers, and private individuals, also speaks to the attractiveness of the market,” AM Best said. Given that private equity firms prioritise high returns on equity, capital-light vehicles are ideal as they allow fronting companies to generate steady, fee-based income by passing the majority of insurance risk along to reinsurers rather than holding it on their own balance sheets. items.rss_title: AI Safety Group METR Finds Flaws in OpenAI’s Internal Monitoring System
items.rss_description: AI safety research group METR said on Thursday a pilot exercise to stress-test OpenAI’s internal monitoring system uncovered several new vulnerabilities, including an exploit that AI agents could have used to keep hundreds of their recent actions from being monitored. …
items.extracted_text: AI Safety Group METR Finds Flaws in OpenAI’s Internal Monitoring System Article 0 Comments AI safety research group METR said on Thursday a pilot exercise to stress-test OpenAI’s internal monitoring system uncovered several new vulnerabilities, including an exploit that AI agents could have used to keep hundreds of their recent actions from being monitored. OpenAI has since said all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards have been patched, though METR said it has not evaluated those claims. The researchers found a way OpenAI’s Codex coding agents could, in principle, bypass safety restrictions and take any action available to the user running them, as well as two settings that could switch off monitoring for new agents. Only about 75% to 94% of OpenAI’s internal AI agent traffic from models at least as powerful as GPT-5.5 was eligible for monitoring, the researchers estimated. The exercise aimed to estimate how much of OpenAI’s AI agent activity was monitored and whether agents could, in principle, disable or get around the system, METR said. It was designed as a pilot for giving outside researchers deep access to a company’s internal systems, the research group added. items.extracted_text: Oklahoma Landlord to Pay $52K for Violating Fair Housing Act Article 0 Comments The Justice Department announced that the owners of a residential rental property in Oklahoma City have agreed to pay $52,500 to resolve a lawsuit alleging that they refused to rent a one-bedroom apartment to a single mother upon learning that she would be living with her child, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. Under the settlement agreement, the defendants must pay $52,500 to the woman who was denied an apartment. The Defendants must also implement a nondiscrimination policy and practices, and undergo training to prevent future discrimination, including familial status discrimination, at The Vintage at Mesta Park. The Department’s lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma in August 2025, alleges that in July 2022 a woman inquired about renting a one-bedroom unit in Defendants’ 36-unit apartment complex known as The Vintage at Mesta Park. The apartment was close to her work, and across the street from a school where she hoped to send her then-three-year-old son. The woman viewed the available unit, a newly remodeled one-bedroom unit, and told Defendants’ rental agent that she wanted to move forward with renting the unit. Defendant Jacqueline Fox, who managed the property and owned the LLC that owns the property, initially told the woman that she would be approved to move in. However, when the woman mentioned that she would be moving in with her son, Defendant Fox responded that the woman could not move in because no children had resided at the property in over eight years, and the property was not “kid friendly.” She refused to rent to the woman and her son, and the woman filed a complaint with the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). HUD referred this case to the Justice Department after HUD received the complaint described above, completed an investigation, and issued a charge of discrimination. The Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing against families with children. Source: Department of Justice Topics Oklahoma Was this article valuable? items.title: Storm Austen Knocks Out Power to Nearly 300,000 French Homes
items.original_title: Storm Austen Knocks Out Power to Nearly 300,000 French Homes
items.rss_title: Storm Austen Knocks Out Power to Nearly 300,000 French Homes
items.rss_description: Storm Austen knocked out electricity to almost 300,000 customers in western France on Friday as hurricane-force winds battered the region, disrupting roads, railways and other transport links.
items.extracted_text: Storm Austen Knocks Out Power to Nearly 300,000 French Homes Article 0 Comments Storm Austen knocked out electricity to almost 300,000 customers in western France on Friday as hurricane-force winds battered the region, disrupting roads, railways and other transport links. Brittany was hardest hit, with almost 150,000 customers without power, according to distributor Enedis. Amber weather alerts are in place across northwest Spain and France, and the western half of Germany. One region in northern Germany near the Harz Mountains is under a red alert for high winds. Airports on Jersey and Guernsey were closed. Cancellations and delays are mounting at Paris airports, according to data from Flight tracking site Flightradar24. Austen is the first named storm this autumn and it’s also sending power prices in France and Germany tumbling. A surge in wind generation is flooding grids with cheap electricity, offering some relief to markets that have been grappling with the highest natural gas prices since the 2022 energy crisis. In Germany, Europe’s biggest power market, wind generation is poised to set a new output record on Friday and could come close to meeting all the nation’s needs on Sunday, although curtailment and must-run generation may limit actual output. Kpler SA forecasts that power prices will drop to €29 a megawatt-hour on Saturday and near zero on Sunday, the lowest since April. French prices are also forecast to plunge, falling to about €17 on Sunday, the lowest since June. The burst of wind generation reduces the need for more expensive gas-fired plants, which often set prices when renewable output is low. Austen swept through the English Channel on Friday, lashing both coasts of France and England with heavy rain. Gusts as high as 140 kilometers per hour (87 miles) are expected in some French coastal areas, equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale, according to Météo-France. Enedis has mobilized more than 2,000 personnel since Wednesday, with several hundred additional technicians being sent to the hardest-hit areas as part of its rapid response force. In Normandy, cuts affected 88,800 customers, 49,600 in Pays de la Loire and almost 8,000 in Hauts-de-France, Enedis said. The storm also disrupted transport across northern and western France. Several roads and train lines around Paris and in Normandy, Brittany and Hauts-de-France were interrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said on X. In the U.K., airports on the Channel Islands of Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney were closed until Friday afternoon. About 20,000 people lost power in southwest England, according to National Grid. The U.K. day-ahead power price for Saturday settled at £37 per megawatt-hour, less than half of the average so far this year according to data from Epex Spot. A second storm, named Boelo, is set to follow this weekend, taking a more northerly route across Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England, according to the U.K. Met Office. Boelo could bring winds of as much as 129 kilometers an hour to coastal areas along with heavy rain. The U.K. has issued amber weather warnings for that storm starting Saturday. The storm patterns could push wind speeds in Europe’s key power markets to 31% above the 10-year average through Nov. 4, helping to offset increased heating demand and weaker solar generation, BloombergNEF said in a note. The rules, which took effect Oct. 18, require insurers to notify policyholders within 30 …
items.extracted_text: Washington Updates Insurance Claims Handling Rules, Deadlines Article 0 Comments New claims handling rules in Washington require insurers to follow updated rules that establish deadlines for responding to policyholders, conducting investigations, issuing denials and making payments. The rules, which took effect Oct. 18, require insurers to notify policyholders within 30 days whether claims have been accepted or denied and provide updates every 30 days if a claim is delayed. The updated rules issued by Washington Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer revise standards for handling claims that had not been updated since their adoption in 1978. The new rules establish specific timelines and documentation requirements for communication, investigations, denials and payments. The prohibit insurers from denying claims without conducting an investigation and state they cannot rely solely on a database for that investigation. Other changes include: Removing language concerning the frequency of unfair claims practices to reinforce that any unfair claims practice can violate state law. Establishing standards for auto damage and total loss claims, including inspection requirements, communications, valuation data sources and handling additional damage. Requiring insurers that use databases to determine pricing or labor rates to provide information about those databases upon request. Policyholders can also request an in-person inspection if they dispute the accuracy of a virtual photo inspection. Requiring insurers to explain claim denials, identify relevant policy provisions, provide vehicle valuation reports and disclose the data sources used in determining vehicle values. The changes follow a 2023 workshop held by the Washington Office of the Insurance Commissioner in response to an increase in auto insurance complaints. More than 80% of complaints filed with the agency leading up to the workshop involved claims handling issues, according to the office. Was this article valuable? items.title: Insurer Doesn’t Get a Mulligan in $12M Georgia Solar Farm Claim, Appeals Court Says
items.original_title: Insurer Doesn’t Get a Mulligan in $12M Georgia Solar Farm Claim, Appeals Court Says
items.rss_title: Insurer Doesn’t Get a Mulligan in $12M Georgia Solar Farm Claim, Appeals Court Says
items.rss_description: Zurich American does not get to reclassify a loss as one with a much higher deductible after it had already paid part of the claim, a federal appeals court said in a case involving rain damage to a massive solar …
items.extracted_text: Insurer Doesn’t Get a Mulligan in $12M Georgia Solar Farm Claim, Appeals Court Says Article 1 Comment Zurich American does not get to reclassify a loss as one with a much higher deductible after it had already paid part of the claim, a federal appeals court said in a case involving rain damage to a massive solar farm in Georgia. “Golfers get mulligans. But in this case, the insurance company does not,” the U.S. 11 th Circuit Court of Appeals wrote in its Oct. 22 opinion. Zurich American had written a builder’s risk policy for First Solar, which was constructing a 200-megawatt solar plant near Warner Robins, in central Georgia, in 2018. Five heavy rain events in 2019 and 2020 left water standing in the former farm field, causing extensive damage to the solar components. A Zurich adjuster determined that the loss was due to water damage, not flooding, and Zurich sent advance payments totaling $600,000 for the first three rainfall events. The policy allowed a $100,000 per-event deductible for water damage. But Zurich then reversed course, arguing that the deluges in 2019 and 2020 were actually flood events. In the policy, flood damage carried a much higher deductible—$2.5 million per event. That meant that all of the claimed damage was below the First Solar policy deductible and no payout was due, Zurich argued, as the court explained. Litigation ensued. After a jury in the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Georgia found in favor of First Solar, the judge awarded $12.2 million, including prejudgment interest. Both sides appealed parts of the decision. A key question was the wording of the policy. Water damage was defined as “all damage caused by water, whatever the source, whether or not driven by wind, other than that otherwise defined as flood or that resulting from a named storm.” Still, Zurich insisted that it was flooding that swamped the solar farm. First Solar’s team at one point argued that because the property was written as being on normally dry land and at least partly in a Level 3 flood area—with only moderate risk of flooding—it had to be considered water damage. Even the solar firm’s insurance agent, John Shaw, got involved, urging Zurich and the adjuster to consider the claim to be caused by water, not flooding. The 11 th Circuit appellate court panel upheld the district court on the first three rain event claims, and remanded the case for more deliberations on the two later rainfalls. The appeals court opinion noted that its reading of the policy and the evidence showed that the higher flood deductible actually applied, in this case. But Zurich had already waived that deductible by paying out on the first three claims as water damage, and by not reserving its rights to change coverage determination, the court decided. “The central question in this appeal is whether Georgia law permits an insurer in Zurich’s situation to take a mulligan—to receive a do-over after messing up the first time,” 11 th Circuit Judge Embry Kidd wrote in the opinion. “Or, under Georgia law, did Zurich’s conduct waive its right to apply the flood deductible after previously applying the water damage deductible?” The answer is “yes:” Zurich waived its right and hooked its tee shot into the woods. No mulligan. The court also found that an oddly worded clause in the policy did not require that legal action had to commence within 12 months of the events. “Accordingly, we conclude that the suit against the company provision is not a suit-limitation provision,” the judges wrote.
